To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the presence of hotspots unrelated to the disease at the end of treatment, the presence of residual non-FDG-avid mass and the presence of bulky disease at baseline PET are the most significant predictors for the occurrence of false-positive findings at PET surveillance.

the use of PET/CT surveillance in asymptomatic patients with HL and NHL in first remission should be restricted to high-risk patients, and that the presence of unrelated hot spots on PET at the end of the treatment can identify a subgroup of patients more likely to show equivocal findings at surveillance PET/CT.

the presence of hot spots unrelated to disease at final PET and previous radiotherapy were the best predictors of a false-positive result, and that a positive PET at 2nd interim PET and the presence of a bulky disease and/or a high maximum standardized uptake value were the best predictors for a true positive result.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of PET/CT for surveillance in lymphoma patients in remission.
the identification of factors predicting the likelihood of relapse and/or FP findings in PETsv.
the use of PET/CT for surveillance in asymptotically lymphoma patients in remission.

PET/CT is not a reliable tool in the management of asymptomatic lymphoma in first remission, and that the decision to perform surveillance PET/CT should be based on a careful risk/benefit assessment.

PET/CT surveillance is useful in patients with a high risk of relapsing and with negative interim PET, but it should be performed with caution in patients with positive interim PET, and should not be used in patients who received previous radiotherapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

PETsv should be restricted to patients at high-risk of relapse, and that the information derived from PET2 and PETsv can help to select patients at higher risk of relapse and patients with a higher likelihood of FP.
PET/CT surveillance in lymphoma patients in remission can be useful, but only if the risk of relapse is high and the patient has a high likelihood of false positive results.

a baseline FDG-PET with a high metabolic tumor burden, an interim PET with a positive finding and a final PET with unrelated hot spots are predictors of false positive findings at surveillance FDG-PETSv.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of surveillance FDG-Pet/CT should be restricted to patients with HL, with high metabolic disease burden at baseline, or with positive interim FDG-PET.
the use of FDG-PET for surveillance in patients with lymphoma in first remission should be restricted to those with high risk of relapses.
the clinical value of surveillance PET/TC is limited, and that its use should be restricted to selected patients.
